description: Lets the running game get on with it and answers when something has happened: a number of frames, a signal, a property reaching a value, or words appearing on a screen. Needs the game running with the runtime addon. Operations: frames (needs frames): let frames pass; signal: wait for a signal and answer with what it carried; watch (needs nodePath, signal): start recording a signal and answer at once with a watch; arm it before the call meant to set the signal off, then collect it with signal and the watch. A client can run a call sent beside a wait only after the wait answers, so a wait sent with the call misses it; until: wait for a property to read as a value, or for words to appear under a node, and answer with what it found; one already true when asked answers at once, with frames 0.

compare.description: until, with a property: how what the property reads stands to value before the wait is met. Default ==. != waits for it to read as anything else. >=, <=, > and < put a number in order, met on the first look past the value or level with it at the precision the property keeps, which is how a counter that steps rather than lands is waited on: a day counter on a fast clock went from 31 to 34 between two looks, and a wait for 32 ran out. For these the value is the number it is rather than fitted to the property, so a fraction on a whole-number property is a threshold rather than refused, and a property holding anything but a number is refused. Only for op until.

frames.description: frames: how many to let pass, 1 to 600. More than that is refused. Only for op frames.

includeHidden.description: until, with says: count words on a hidden node too. Default false, since a wait for words is a wait for them to be shown: a button that exists hidden through a whole animation carries its words the whole time and satisfied the wait at once, and every wait on that screen fell back to counting frames. Only for op until.

nodePath.description: signal, watch, until: the node. Needed for a signal without a watch, a watch and a property; for says it defaults to /root, the whole screen. Only for ops signal, watch, until.

pid.description: Which game, when several are running from one project, such as a bench and its workers: its process id, as editor_status lists under runtimes. Without it the game this server started or plays is the one asked when it is among them, and the answer says so under answeredBy; with one game per project it is not needed at all.

projectPath.description: Which game, when more than one is running: the project directory it was started from. The pick without it, in order: the game this server started or is playing when it is among those running, named under answeredBy where there was a choice; else the only game there is; else a refusal naming every game and which argument tells them apart, pid when they are all one project and projectPath when they are not. Not needed with one game, nor for a call to this server's own.

property.description: until: the property name, or a colon path through what the node holds, "_game:run:day", read the way runtime_inspect property reads one, a step written as a call included, and one axis of a vector as well: "global_position:x" with compare ">=" stops once a thing has travelled far enough. Walked again on every frame, so a holder the game replaces while the wait is on is followed. Only for op until.

says.description: until: wait for these words to appear anywhere under nodePath, or anywhere in the game when no nodePath is given, instead of for a property, which is how a panel that rebuilds its labels is waited on at all: the labels are named afresh each redraw and the panel is what stays put. Matched the way runtime_inspect find matches says: case-insensitive, a plain word anywhere in the text, a pattern with * or ? a glob over the whole of it, and alternatives separated by | met by whichever appears first ("*won*|*lost*"); on a node the player can see unless includeHidden says otherwise; a label with a line break is matched with the break in the words, and a backslash followed by n counts as one. Instead of, not as well as: a call carrying this and a property is refused, because they ask about different things and answering one of them silently is how a caller watches a screen believing they are watching a property. It looks every frame while a look is cheap and less often on a screen large enough for a look to cost a real share of a frame, so the game keeps its speed; the answer counts the frames the wait spanned and the looks it took, and says under looking_ms how long the looks took between them. Only for op until.

signal.description: signal, watch: the signal name. Only for ops signal, watch.

timeoutMs.description: signal, until: how long to wait before answering anyway, 1 to 120000. Default 5000. Only for ops signal, until.

value.description: until: the value to wait for, fitted to the property's type and compared at the precision the property keeps, so -1.1 meets a 32-bit float holding -1.10000002. A value the property would have to cut is refused: a fraction on a whole number, a number other than 0 or 1 on a bool. On a property holding an object, whether declared to or untyped and holding one or null, the text null means null. One declared to hold an object refuses any value other than null, since it can never hold it. Only for op until.

watch.description: signal: the watch an earlier watch answered, in place of nodePath and signal. Answers at once, with fired_before_wait, when the signal fired after the watch was armed, and otherwise waits for it; times counts how often it fired, and args is what the first carried. The watch goes with the answer. Only for op signal.

name: runtime_wait
title: Wait in the running game
